settings.prompt:
Autonomously review this Java source repository for potential security
vulnerabilities using the available read-only tools. Do not ask the user questions or summarize
tool output. Copy exact relative paths from list_files or index results; never invent or prefix a path.
A file listing or index hint is only navigation; inspect original source and seek
counter-evidence before deciding. Trace plausible untrusted input to security-sensitive
operations where possible, and check relevant guards and configuration. Report at most 10
candidates supported by exact source lines, with root cause, preconditions, counter-evidence,
and missing evidence. Do not assume a vulnerability exists. If source review finds no supported
candidate, submit an empty candidate list. Your final action must be submit_findings; natural
language commentary is not a report. Do not use project names, dataset identifiers, or a guessed
known answer as evidence.

counter_evidence: The reconstructed instance is cast to (XMLInputFactory) / (XMLOutputFactory) at XmlFactory.java lines 191-192, which constrains which classes can be the resulting factory and would cause ClassCastException for most unrelated gadget classes.
This path is only reachable through JDK serialization (readObject/readResolve); it is not reachable from normal XML parse/serialize flows.
The writeObject path (lines 220-224) stores the actual factory class names, so for legitimately-serialized factories readResolve simply restores the same implementation.
candidates.description: XmlFactory implements Java serialization hooks. writeObject() stores the class names of the in-use XMLInputFactory/XMLOutputFactory (lines 220-224). readObject() reads those two UTF strings back from the stream (lines 208-214), and readResolve() then reconstructs the factories via Class.forName(_jdkXmlInFactory).newInstance() and Class.forName(_jdkXmlOutFactory).newInstance() (lines 190-192). Class names therefore originate from attacker-controllable serialized input if an XmlFactory (or a structure containing it) is deserialized from an untrusted source. This allows an attacker who can supply a serialized object stream to force loading and no-arg instantiation of any class name that is on the classpath and matches the XMLInputFactory/XMLOutputFactory cast, and more generally demonstrates the classic risk of JDK deserialization of this type. Root cause: trusting names embedded in Java-serialized data to drive class loading/instantiation, rather than validating against a safe/expected allowlist or reconstructing a fixed implementation. Note the immediate effect is bounded by the cast to XMLInputFactory/XMLOutputFactory performed in readResolve before the returned instance is used, so exploitation is not established by source review alone.
missing_evidence: No code in the repository shows whether/how XmlFactory is exposed to JDK deserialization of untrusted data (no readObject call sites were found in main sources).
No evidence of an exploitable gadget chain or of a classpath where an attacker-controlled XMLInputFactory/XMLOutputFactory implementation yields code execution.
No tests or docs establish the intended trust boundary for serialized XmlFactory instances.
preconditions: Application deserializes Java-serialized objects (ObjectInputStream.readObject) containing an XmlFactory, or an object graph that includes one, from an untrusted/attacker-influenced source.
Attacker can control the two UTF-strings written into/hidden in the serialized stream that are read into _jdkXmlInFactory / _jdkXmlOutFactory.
A class name that (a) implements javax.xml.stream.XMLInputFactory or XMLOutputFactory, or otherwise satisfies the cast, is present on the application classpath.
candidates.title: XmlFactory.readResolve() instantiates arbitrary classes from JDK-deserialized factory names (Class.forName/newInstance on serialized data)

counter_evidence: The library exposes setXMLInputFactory(XMLInputFactory) (lines 340-342) and XmlMapper(XMLInputFactory) / XmlMapper(XMLInputFactory, XMLOutputFactory) constructors (XmlMapper.java lines 55-64), letting applications supply a hardened factory and overriding the defaults.

Only IS_COALESCING and IS_REPAIRING_NAMESPACES are set, leaving the security-relevant properties at provider default; many providers (e.g. recent Woodstox) default to not resolving external general entities, which would mitigate XXE.
No code path in this repository was observed actually enabling external entity resolution or DTD support.
candidates.description: XmlFactory._initFactories() configures the XMLInputFactory with only IS_COALESCING=true (line 141) and the XMLOutputFactory with IS_REPAIRING_NAMESPACES=true (line 139). No attempt is made to set security-relevant StAX properties such as XMLInputFactory.SUPPORT_DTD, IS_SUPPORTING_EXTERNAL_ENTITIES, or IS_REPLACING_ENTITY_REFERENCES to restrict external-entity / DTD expansion. All parser-creation paths (_createParser for InputStream/Reader/char[]/byte[] and createParser(XMLStreamReader), lines 532-604 and 486-504) delegate to _xmlInputFactory.createXMLStreamReader(...), so the resulting XXE/billion-laughs exposure is entirely a function of the underlying StAX provider defaults and whatever the caller configures. When callers use the default XmlFactory()/XmlMapper() (XmlMapper.java lines 48-50, 66-68), the provider is obtained via XMLInputFactory.newInstance() (XmlFactory.java lines 112-114) with no hardening applied by this library. This is a configuration/hardening gap rather than a demonstrated vulnerability: with hardened providers (e.g. Woodstox defaults, or explicit ExternalEntity/DTD disabling) the gap may be irrelevant.
missing_evidence: No code or configuration in the repository pins/selects a specific StAX provider for the production runtime, so the effective (provider-specific) default for SUPPORT_DTD and external entity resolution cannot be determined from source alone.
No test in the repository exercises external entities / DOCTYPE to show whether they are resolved or blocked.
No evidence that DTD/entity features were intentionally omitted versus delegated to callers.
preconditions: Application uses default XmlMapper()/XmlFactory() construction (or otherwise does not pre-configure/harden the XMLInputFactory).
The selected StAX provider's defaults leave DTD processing and/or external entity resolution enabled for the deployment.
Untrusted XML is parsed (e.g. readValue from a request body) such that a DOCTYPE with external/internal entities can be supplied.
candidates.title: StAX parser configured only with IS_COALESCING; DTD/entity-expansion hardening settings are left to provider defaults
